clues.title: Landscape: grassland, gentle hills, overcast
text: This is the stereotypical Uruguay round. The coverage often, but not always, features **overcast** weather. Most of the landscape consists of open grasslands with gentle hills. Occasionally, you might see separated tree plantations. Roads are generally in worse condition than in neighbouring countries.

images.caption: Gravel road through open grassland, with text notes on tree plantations, overcast weather, gentle hills and road quality

clues.summary: Open grassland with gentle hills, often under overcast skies, with the odd block of planted trees. Roads are in worse shape than in neighbouring countries.

clues.title: Plate: plain white, black characters
text: Uruguayan **licence plates** are plain white with black characters.
NOTE: Neighbouring Argentina also uses white licence plates, but they will have either a black dot in the middle or a blue bar at the top.

images.caption: Uruguayan plates: standard and from March 2015

clues.summary: Plain white plates with black characters. Argentine plates are also white but have a black dot in the middle or a blue bar on top.

differs.how: Argentine plates have a black dot or a blue top bar

clues.title: Google car: black car, no antenna
text: Uruguay only has Generation 3 coverage. Coverage was taken by a **black Google car** without an antenna.
The car is [not always visible](https://goo.gl/maps/KnYb3vpU7r7n6sKi8).
NOTE: Within South America, you can also find this car in Argentina and Peru.
clues.summary: Only older Gen 3 coverage, shot by a black car with no antenna. The car is not always visible. Argentina and Peru used the same car.

clues.title: Coverage: smudgy picture quality
text: In a lot of coverage, the camera quality is somewhat **smudgy**.
NOTE: This is significantly less common in Argentina.
clues.summary: Much of the coverage looks somewhat smudgy. Argentina has this much less often.

clues.title: Direction sign: thick white wooden post
text: Uruguay uses **thick wooden signposts**, which are typically painted white. They often have up to four rectangular notches at the back of the post.
NOTE: Thick wooden signposts can also be seen in Bolivia.
clues.summary: Thick wooden signposts, usually painted white, often with up to four rectangular notches at the back. Bolivia has thick wooden posts too.

clues.title: Road lines: yellow double with white dashes
text: Uruguay often has these **triple road lines**, that consist of double yellow roadlines with white dashes in between. This is a design not seen anywhere else in the Americas.
clues.summary: Triple road lines: a double yellow line with white dashes between. Not seen anywhere else in the Americas.

clues.title: Road lines: yellow-white or plain white
text: You can also find two other, non-unique road line patterns:
- Yellow-white lines (also found in Argentina)
- Simple white lines (found in many other places).
clues.summary: Two other patterns that are not unique: yellow-white lines (also in Argentina) and simple white lines (found in many places).

clues.title: Bollard: white post, one side yellow
text: These **white bollards**, with one side often painted [yellow](https://goo.gl/maps/Tt64mBZvxz5qYZhv9), and **stone barriers**, are specific to Uruguay.
clues.summary: White bollards, often with one side painted yellow, and stone barriers. Both are specific to this country.

clues.title: Pole: trident, three upward insulators
text: Uruguay uses a handful of different utility poles. One very common and useful one are the so-called **trident poles**, which get their name from their distinctive pole tops with three insulators that point upwards.
NOTE: Similar trident poles can be found in the neighbouring Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul.

images.caption: Pole against the sky; the red circle zooms in on a trident top with three upward insulators

clues.summary: A very common pole with three insulators pointing up like a trident. The same type exists in the neighbouring Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul.

differs.how: Only in the far south of Brazil, next to the border

clues.title: Pole: flat metal sheets top or square concrete
text: You can also see a variety of other pole designs, including:
- Round poles with a pole top consisting of **flat metal sheets**
- **Square** concrete poles.
Both of these pole designs are also good clues for Uruguay.
In addition, you might see simple wooden poles with [one insulator](https://goo.gl/maps/7xGVU84ikAnmChmB7), as well as very rarely some [Argentina-style poles](https://goo.gl/maps/q6KAW3fKBVBTH79q9).

images.caption: Two poles; red circles zoom in on a flat metal-sheet top and a square concrete pole

clues.summary: Round poles topped with flat metal sheets, and square concrete poles, are both good clues. You may also see simple wooden poles with one insulator and, very rarely, Argentine-style poles.

differs.how: Argentine poles are rare here and look different

clues.title: Guardrail: small reflector, 3.5-sided support
text: Uruguayan guardrails have a small, rectangular yellow or red reflector, which is the same as in Argentina. They can be differentiated by the shape of their [support](/images/uruguay/argentinauruguay_guardrailsupport.jpg).
In Argentina, the supports are made up of three sides of a rectangle. Uruguayan supports have the same three sides, and additionally parts of the fourth side at the corners.

images.caption: Small reflector on the guardrail, zoomed in the red circles

clues.summary: A small rectangular yellow or red reflector, as in Argentina. Tell them apart by the support: Argentine ones have three sides of a rectangle, Uruguayan ones also have bits of the fourth side at the corners.

differs.how: Support has exactly three sides of a rectangle

clues.title: Kilometre marker: green-painted stone
text: This **green-painted** stone kilometre marker is unique to Uruguay.

images.caption: A green-painted stone kilometre marker beside the road

clues.summary: A stone kilometre marker painted green. Unique here.

clues.title: Chevron: yellow with black arrows
text: Like most of Latin America, chevrons are **yellow with black arrows**.
NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish between Argentina, which uniquely uses chevrons that are white with red arrows.
clues.summary: Yellow chevrons with black arrows, like most of Latin America. Useful mainly to rule out Argentina, which uses white with red arrows.

differs.how: Argentine chevrons are white with red arrows

clues.title: Landscape: subtle hills, never flat
text: As mentioned before, most of Uruguay is **slightly hilly**, even though the overall elevation is fairly low. Although it is by no means a mountainous country, roads generally have at least a slight incline.
Take note that this hilliness is usually very subtle: don’t expect immense rolling hills in most of the country.
NOTE: If your location is completely flat, consider that you might be in Argentina instead.
clues.summary: Most of the country is slightly hilly even though it's low. Roads usually have at least a slight incline, but the hills are subtle. If it's totally flat, think Argentina.

differs.how: Argentine pampas can be completely flat

clues.title: Soil: reddish, light pink to deep red
text: In many parts of Uruguay, you can find **reddish soil**. The tint can range from light pink (pictured here) to [deep red](https://goo.gl/maps/64EEWrb8oLht4QVB7).
NOTE: This type of reddish soil is less common in the similar-looking parts of Argentina. Hence, it can be a good clue for Uruguay when you are faced with a tough decision.

However, be cautious with using this meta in the inverse way: the absence of this type of soil does not exclude Uruguay, as you can still find a lot of generic [white](https://goo.gl/maps/18MHSuQW8WQZU6nM8) and [brown](https://goo.gl/maps/CvDfgvEs1vxAUejM6) soil throughout the country.
clues.summary: Reddish soil, from light pink to deep red, is common. It is rarer in similar parts of Argentina, so it helps in a tough call. White and brown soil also occurs, so its absence rules nothing out.

differs.how: Reddish soil is less common there

clues.title: Houses: boxy concrete, drab, flat roofs
text: Many **Uruguayan houses** are made out of concrete, and are somewhat cube-shaped. Walls often have drab colours and tend to look weathered. Flat roofs are relatively common.
NOTE: Architecture in Argentina often looks similar.
clues.summary: Many houses are cube-shaped concrete with drab, weathered colours and often flat roofs. Argentine houses often look similar.

clues.title: Plants: short stocky palm trees
text: Occasionally, you might see **palm trees**. These short and stocky species of palm tree are particularly common.
clues.summary: Short, stocky palm trees are an occasional sight.

clues.title: Landscape: lots of cattle
text: **Cattle farming** is an important part of Uruguay’s agriculture. Cattle outnumber people four by one, so you will see a lot of them around in rural rounds.

images.caption: Cattle grazing in a green field

clues.summary: Cattle outnumber people about four to one, so you see plenty of them in the countryside.

clues.title: Coverage: limited, mostly main roads
text: **Coverage** in Uruguay is somewhat limited. The densest coverage is in the south, in and around Montevideo. Outside of this area, most coverage is confined to yellow roads. This makes **angle guessing** a powerful tool to potentially get very close guesses.
For a zoomable overview of official street view coverage, [see this site](https://sv-map.netlify.app/#base=roadmap&cov=official&zoom=7&center=-32.46354529706703%2C-55.93139648437501).
clues.summary: Coverage is thin. The densest is in the south around the capital; elsewhere it follows the yellow main roads, so guessing the road angle can get you very close.

clues.title: Landscape: tallest hills in two spots
text: Subtle differences in **elevation** can help when trying to region-guess Uruguay.
The highest hills are mostly concentrated around two areas:
- Near Minas, east of Montevideo.
- North of Tacuarembo, in the far north of the country.
clues.summary: The highest hills are in two areas: near Minas, east of the capital, and north of Tacuarembó in the far north. Use subtle height differences to region-guess.

clues.title: Landscape: tall hills, exposed rocks, bushland
text: The landscape near the town of Minas is recognizable: some of the **tallest hills** in the country, with lots of **exposed rocks**, and often [heavy bushland vegetation](https://goo.gl/maps/1ZNebpfyoL27cq6C9).
The image shown here is a fairly extreme example of this landscape, used for illustration purposes – usually it is more subtle. However, the exposed rock is always a good clue.

NOTE: The landscape in the Quebrada de los Cuervos nature reserve, situated further north, [can look similar](https://goo.gl/maps/eaDMYgJxi43cnmJK9). In addition, there are also very tall hills in the north of the country. However, these look different (see the tip below).
clues.summary: Around Minas are some of the tallest hills here with lots of bare rock and heavy bushes. Usually more subtle than the example. Bare rock is always a good clue. The Quebrada de los Cuervos reserve further north can look similar.

clues.title: Landscape: tall hills with darker soil
text: You can also find tall hills in the north of the country. These can be recognized by their noticeably **darker soil**. These hills also typically do not have the exposed rocks that are visible in the Minas hills.
The vegetation tends to be natural, and you will often see **tree plantations**.
This specific landscape tends to be most noticeable very close to the Brazil border, on Route 30 near Tranqueras.
clues.summary: In the north, tall hills with noticeably darker soil, natural vegetation and often tree plantations. No bare rocks like in the Minas hills. Strongest near the Brazil border on Route 30 near Tranqueras.

differs.how: Brazilian side looks similar, so check signs and plates

clues.title: Plants: tree plantations
text: **Tree plantations** are a defining feature of much of Uruguay’s countryside, but they are especially common in two areas in the north and northwest.
Note that the highest density of plantations is in these areas, but more isolated plantations can be found all over the country.
clues.summary: Planted tree blocks are common in the countryside, densest in two areas in the north and northwest, with isolated ones all over.

clues.title: Landscape: very flat southeast near Brazil
text: The region near Lagoa Mirim and the Brazil border in the southeast of the country is noticeably **very flat**, in contrast to the slight hills found in most of the rest of the country.
clues.summary: The southeast near Lagoa Mirim and the Brazil border is very flat, unlike the gentle hills in most of the country.

differs.how: Same flat land continues across the border

clues.title: Road: divided highway
text: There are only a couple of **divided highways** in Uruguay, all of which are close to Montevideo:
- Ruta 1 going west out of Montevideo, up until Colonia Valdense.
- Ruta IB going east out of Montevideo, up until Punta del Este.
- A short section of Ruta 5 going north out of Montevideo, up until Canelones.
The only exceptions to this are some divided avenues in urban areas, which should be easy to distinguish from actual highways.
clues.summary: Divided highways are rare and all near the capital: Ruta 1 west to Colonia Valdense, Ruta IB east to Punta del Este and a short bit of Ruta 5 north to Canelones.

clues.title: Bins: orange lids
text: These bins with **orange lids are** specific to Rocha Department. However, you can still find these [black bins](https://goo.gl/maps/6evWkb48DFNw31847) in both the Rocha and Canelones Department.

images.caption: A bin with an orange lid on a dirt verge

clues.summary: Bins with orange lids are only in Rocha Department. Black bins appear in both Rocha and Canelones.

clues.title: Landscape: dense big-city sprawl
text: **Montevideo** is by far the largest city in Uruguay. More than half the Uruguayan population lives within its metropolitan area.

Its relatively massive size may not always be as apparent in its suburbs. However, if you are in a densely populated, highly built-up area, consider guessing in downtown Montevideo, as there are very few places like that in other parts of Uruguay.

images.caption: A dense big-city street between tall buildings

clues.summary: The capital is by far the biggest city; over half the population lives in its area. If you are somewhere very dense and built-up, guess the capital, since few places elsewhere look like that.

clues.title: Houses: tall modern flats by a sandy beach
text: **Punta del Este** is a seaside resort town with a recognizable look. It is an affluent and touristic place with a developed downtown that consists of many tall, modern apartment buildings. Its main attraction is its large, sandy beach.

Further away from the downtown area, you will see less highrises, but still a lot of expensive-looking villa neighbourhoods. Here, you will often see distinctive [tall pine trees](https://goo.gl/maps/9cKem7TVVuhbksbE8).
clues.summary: A rich seaside resort town with many tall modern apartment blocks and a big sandy beach. Further out are expensive villas and tall pine trees.

clues.title: Coverage: small island trekker, lighthouse
text: The small island of **Isla de Flores** is located off the coast of Montevideo. It has a trekker where you can see abandoned buildings, and usually also the lighthouse.
clues.summary: Isla de Flores, a small island off the capital, has a walking-camera trek showing abandoned buildings and usually the lighthouse.

clues.title: Google car: orange strap on the left
text: This unique Google car is found in the coastal town of **Cabo Polonio**. It can be recognized by the orange strap on the left.

The coverage is an off-road trekker line on the map. The town that it drives through has a unique vibe, consisting of [makeshift-looking shacks](https://goo.gl/maps/kFRyFRU2vKYk4qUc6), scattered around the seaside landscape. In some of the coverage, the car drives [on the beach](https://goo.gl/maps/TcgFWK775WANzTax8).

images.caption: An orange strap hangs on the left of the car's blur

clues.summary: A unique off-road trekker in the coastal town of Cabo Polonio, with an orange strap on the left. It passes makeshift-looking shacks by the sea and sometimes drives on the beach.

clues.title: Google car: white front, curved black back
text: This unique Google car is found in the **Valle del Lunarejo** natural park, located west of the town of Tranqueras. The car has a white front and a curved black backside with a brown strap.
The coverage is an off-road trekker line on the map. The car drives on a small track through a [grassy landscape](https://goo.gl/maps/uBVaJPJwiV9Ks2UX6).
NOTE: This park only shows up as a point of interest on the map, instead of the usual dark green polygon used for natural parks.
clues.summary: A unique off-road trekker in Valle del Lunarejo park, west of Tranqueras. The car has a white front and curved black back with a brown strap, on a small track through grassland. The park shows as a point on the map, not a green area.
